title: Replication, backups, failover and pooling
scopeHtml: Scope: streaming and logical replication, lag, backups, PITR, failover, PgBouncer connection pooling. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: Why replicate
notes.html:
Replication keeps copies of the database on other machines. Three separate reasons, each with different requirements:

  1. High availability: if the primary dies, a copy takes over.
  2. Read scaling: send read-only queries to replicas.
  3. Backup and analytics isolation: run heavy reports on a copy so they do not slow production.

Single-writer model (Postgres default): one primary accepts writes; replicas are read-only copies that continuously apply the primary's changes. Multi-writer is a different, much harder world (file 11).

Worked example. A product has 2,000 reads/s and 100 writes/s. A single primary handles both, but peak reads reach 8,000/s. Add 2 replicas and route reads: each replica serves ~4,000/s; primary stays at 100 writes/s plus WAL shipping. Cost is a few extra instances; the risk is stale reads (replica lag).

Industry examples. Instagram and GitHub ran large primary-plus-replicas fleets for years. Most managed Postgres (RDS, Cloud SQL, Aurora) offers one-click read replicas.

Everyday analogy. A master recipe book and photocopies in each kitchen: copies are updated after the master, so a copy can be a page behind.

Common interview traps.

  • Assuming replicas help write throughput. They do not.
  • Forgetting that every replica must replay all writes, so replica CPU/IO must handle the write rate.

notes.title: Streaming (physical) replication
notes.html:
Physical streaming replication ships the primary's WAL records over TCP to standbys, which replay them byte for byte. The standby is an exact binary copy: same version, same architecture, whole cluster (all databases).

Setup essentials:

# primary postgresql.conf
wal_level = replica
max_wal_senders = 10
max_replication_slots = 10
hot_standby = on            # standby allows read-only queries
# standby bootstrap
pg_basebackup -h primary -U replicator -D /var/lib/postgresql/16/main \
  -R -X stream --slot=replica1
# -R writes standby.signal and primary_conninfo for you

Replication slots make the primary keep WAL until the standby has received it, so a lagging or disconnected standby does not lose its place. Danger: an abandoned slot makes WAL pile up until the disk fills (use max_slot_wal_keep_size).

Synchronous vs asynchronous.

  • Async (default): COMMIT returns after the local WAL flush; a replica may miss the last transactions if the primary dies (small data loss: RPO > 0).
  • Sync: synchronous_standby_names = 'FIRST 1 (replica1, replica2)'; COMMIT also waits for a standby; RPO = 0 but commit latency now includes a network round trip (~1 to 2 ms in one region, 50 ms+ cross-region), and if all sync standbys are down, writes block.

Measuring lag:

-- on primary
SELECT application_name, state, sync_state,
       pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), replay_lsn) AS bytes_behind,
       replay_lag
FROM pg_stat_replication;

Decision gravity. Sync vs async is an availability-vs-durability dial and reversible via config. Choosing a quorum like ANY 1 (a,b) keeps writes going if one standby dies.

Everyday analogy. A court stenographer sending live transcripts to a second office. Sync means the judge waits for the second office to confirm each line.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing sync replication means reads from the replica are always fresh (replay can still lag: remote_apply solves that).
  • Leaving a dead replication slot.
  • Confusing physical (binary, same major version) with logical replication.

notes.title: Replica lag and read-your-writes
notes.html:
Replica lag is the delay between a commit on the primary and its visibility on a replica. Normally milliseconds; under load, long queries on the replica, or network trouble it can reach seconds or minutes.

Symptom the user sees: "I posted a comment, refreshed, and it is gone." (stale read). Fixes (read-your-writes):

  1. Read from the primary for a short time (e.g. 5 s) after the user writes (session flag or cookie).
  2. Pass the LSN: after a write, read pg_current_wal_lsn(); route the following read to a replica only when pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() >= that LSN.
  3. Use synchronous_commit = remote_apply for critical flows.
  4. Make the UI optimistic (show the new comment locally).

Replica conflicts. A long query on a replica can clash with WAL replay that removes rows the query still needs. Postgres either cancels the query (max_standby_streaming_delay, default 30 s) or delays replay. hot_standby_feedback = on tells the primary to keep those rows, at the cost of primary bloat.

Worked example. A nightly report runs 40 minutes on replica 2. With default settings, replay pauses up to 30 s and then the query is cancelled with "canceling statement due to conflict with recovery". Options: a dedicated reporting replica with max_standby_streaming_delay = -1 (unbounded, lag grows) and no user traffic.

Industry examples. Facebook-style systems tag requests with write timestamps/LSNs; Rails has automatic multi-database role switching with a "delay after write" window.

Everyday analogy. Posting a letter and immediately asking the neighbour whether it has arrived.

Common interview traps.

  • Sending all reads to replicas without addressing stale reads after writes.
  • Not monitoring lag (replay_lag) or alerting on it.

notes.title: Logical replication
notes.html:
Logical replication ships row-level changes (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) decoded from the WAL, per table, using publish/subscribe. Unlike physical replication, the target can be a different major version, a subset of tables, or even a different system.

-- publisher
CREATE PUBLICATION app_pub FOR TABLE orders, customers;
-- subscriber
CREATE SUBSCRIPTION app_sub
  CONNECTION 'host=old dbname=app user=repl'
  PUBLICATION app_pub;

Needs wal_level = logical. Caveats: tables need a primary key (or replica identity); DDL and sequences are not replicated automatically; large transactions are slow to apply.

Uses:

  • Zero-downtime major upgrades: subscribe a new-version server, let it catch up, then switch the app.
  • CDC: Debezium reads the logical decoding stream and publishes to Kafka.
  • Selective copies: feed an analytics database.

Industry examples. Many companies upgrade Postgres 12 to 16 using logical replication with a few seconds of cutover. Shopify and others use CDC streams to build search indexes and caches.

Decision gravity. Physical for HA and read scaling (simple, complete); logical for upgrades, partial replication and event streams. Logical slots, like physical ones, retain WAL if the consumer stalls.

Everyday analogy. Physical is photocopying the whole book page by page; logical is sending a list of "change line 4 to X" edits for chosen chapters.

Common interview traps.

  • Assuming logical replication copies schema changes.
  • Using logical replication for failover without handling sequences.

notes.title: Backups: logical and physical
notes.html:
A backup you have never restored is not a backup. Two families:

Logical (pg_dump) Physical (pg_basebackup, snapshots)
Output SQL or custom-format dump of objects Copy of data files plus WAL
Restore speed Slow (re-inserts, rebuilds indexes) Fast (copy back, replay WAL)
Cross-version Yes No (same major)
Granularity One table or schema possible Whole cluster
PITR No Yes with WAL archive 
# logical, parallel, custom format
pg_dump -Fd -j 4 -f /backups/app_2026-11-09 appdb
pg_restore -j 4 -d appdb_restored /backups/app_2026-11-09

# physical base backup
pg_basebackup -D /backups/base -Ft -z -X stream -P

Worked example. 1 TB database: pg_dump + restore takes hours (rebuilding indexes dominates); a physical base backup copies at, say, 200 MB/s, about 1.5 hours, and restore is the same plus WAL replay. A cloud volume snapshot is near instant to create (copy-on-write) but you must handle consistency (Postgres crash-consistent snapshot plus WAL is usually safe; confirm with your provider's docs).

Rules (the 3-2-1 idea). 3 copies, 2 different media, 1 off-site/off-account. Encrypt backups, test restores on a schedule, and protect backups from the same ransomware or accidental-delete path as production.

Tools. pgBackRest, Barman, WAL-G handle base backups, WAL archiving, retention, compression, encryption and parallel restore to S3/GCS.

Everyday analogy. A fire drill: owning an extinguisher is not enough, you need to have practised using it.

Common interview traps.

  • Never testing restores.
  • Keeping backups on the same disk or account as the database.
  • Believing replicas are backups (a bad DELETE replicates instantly).

notes.title: Point-in-time recovery (PITR)
notes.html:
PITR restores the database to any moment (for example 10:41:59, just before a bad DELETE) by restoring a base backup and replaying archived WAL up to a target.

Setup:

# postgresql.conf on primary
archive_mode = on
archive_command = 'pgbackrest --stanza=main archive-push %p'

Recovery:

# on the restored host, then create recovery.signal
restore_command = 'pgbackrest --stanza=main archive-get %f "%p"'
recovery_target_time = '2026-11-09 10:41:59+00'
recovery_target_action = 'promote'

Metrics: RPO (how much data you can lose) is bounded by WAL archive frequency (or zero with streaming plus sync standby). RTO (how long recovery takes) = restore time + replay time. For 1 TB with weekly full + daily incremental backups and 20 MB/s WAL, RTO is perhaps 1 to 3 hours (illustrative); shortening it means more frequent base backups or a warm standby.

Worked example (incident). At 10:42 an engineer runs DELETE FROM orders without WHERE. Steps: stop writes to prevent more damage, restore the latest base backup onto a NEW server, replay WAL to 10:41:59, then dump the missing rows from the recovered copy and re-insert into production (or swap). Time: ~2 hours, and all other writes after 10:42 on prod are preserved if you copy rows instead of swapping.

Industry examples. GitLab's 2017 database incident (public postmortem) is the canonical lesson: five backup methods, none working when needed. Managed services expose "restore to point in time" built on exactly this.

Decision gravity. Retention (7 vs 35 days) is a cost-vs-safety dial and easy to change; archiving WAL must be enabled before you need it, since you cannot recover to a moment that was not archived.

Everyday analogy. A video recording with save points: rewind to the last save, then fast-forward to just before the mistake.

Common interview traps.

  • No WAL archiving, so only restore-to-backup-time is possible.
  • Replaying to a time after the damage.
  • Forgetting RTO includes validation and cutover, not just restore.

notes.title: Failover and high availability
notes.html:
Failover is promoting a standby to primary when the primary fails, then redirecting clients. Manual failover takes minutes and mistakes; automated tools do it in about 10 to 30 s.

Pieces:

  1. Failure detection (missed heartbeats, usually a few seconds to avoid false triggers).
  2. Leader election with a consensus store (etcd/Consul/ZooKeeper) so only ONE node becomes primary. Without it you get split brain: two primaries accepting writes and diverging data.
  3. Promotion (pg_promote()), then other standbys follow the new primary (pg_rewind can fix the old primary to rejoin).
  4. Client routing: virtual IP, DNS with short TTL, HAProxy/PgBouncer, or a managed endpoint.
  5. Fencing: make sure the old primary cannot take writes (STONITH: shut the node down, remove its network).

Tools: Patroni (etcd-based, the de facto standard for self-managed), repmgr, Stolon; managed services (RDS Multi-AZ, Aurora, Cloud SQL HA) hide all this.

Worked example. Primary dies at 12:00:00. etcd leader key TTL 30 s, loop_wait 10 s, retry_timeout 10 s. At about 12:00:30 a standby (most up-to-date, sync) grabs the key, promotes in ~1 s, HAProxy health checks switch in ~5 s. Total about 35 s of unavailability; with async replication up to the lag worth of commits may be lost. RTO ~35 s; RPO depends on sync mode.

Incident pattern. False failover: a network blip makes the primary look dead, a standby promotes, the old primary is alive and still receiving some clients: split brain. Prevent with fencing, a quorum store and a lease that the old primary must renew to keep serving.

Decision gravity. Automatic failover is a trade: faster recovery vs risk of wrong promotion. Choose thresholds with data. Cross-region failover is a bigger one-way operational decision (DNS, data loss window, client config).

Everyday analogy. A captain going overboard: the crew must agree on exactly one new captain, and the old captain must not keep issuing orders from the water.

Common interview traps.

  • Describing failover without fencing or consensus.
  • Saying failover is zero downtime. It is seconds to tens of seconds.
  • Ignoring that apps must reconnect and retry.

notes.title: Connection pooling
notes.html:
Every Postgres connection is an OS process (about 5 to 10 MB baseline, more with work_mem usage), so thousands of connections hurt. Practical sweet spot: roughly 2 to 4 active connections per CPU core. A pooler multiplexes many client connections over a small set of server connections.

PgBouncer modes:

  • Session: a server connection is held for the whole client session. Safest, least multiplexing.
  • Transaction: server connection held only during a transaction. Best multiplexing (the usual choice) but breaks session state: session-level advisory locks, SET without LOCAL, LISTEN/NOTIFY, and (historically) protocol-level prepared statements. Check your PgBouncer version for prepared-statement support.
  • Statement: one statement at a time; rarely usable.
; pgbouncer.ini
[databases]
app = host=10.0.0.5 port=5432 dbname=app

[pgbouncer]
pool_mode = transaction
max_client_conn = 5000
default_pool_size = 40        ; server connections per db/user pair
reserve_pool_size = 5
server_idle_timeout = 600

Worked example. 100 app pods x 20 pool connections = 2,000 connections hitting a 16-core Postgres: context switching, memory, and max_connections limits. Put PgBouncer in front with default_pool_size = 40: 2,000 client connections share 40 server connections, CPU drops, latency improves. Also size app-side pools small (e.g. HikariCP maximumPoolSize 10) since a large app pool does not make the database faster.

Incident pattern. Deploy restarts 100 pods; each opens connections at once: "too many clients already" or a connection storm. Metric: pg_stat_activity count versus max_connections; mitigate with a pooler, slow starts and max_connections headroom.

Industry examples. Supabase, Heroku, and many SaaS vendors run PgBouncer or Odyssey/pgcat in front of Postgres; AWS RDS Proxy is the managed analogue.

Everyday analogy. A restaurant with 10 waiters for 200 diners: you do not hire one waiter per diner.

Common interview traps.

  • Raising max_connections to 5,000 instead of pooling.
  • Using session-level features through a transaction-mode pooler.
  • Forgetting the pooler is itself a component to make highly available.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Replication serves availability, read scaling and isolation; Postgres is single-writer; replicas do not raise write throughput.
  • Physical streaming replication ships WAL; async risks losing recent commits, sync costs a network round trip and can block writes.
  • Replica lag causes stale reads; solve with read-your-writes routing, LSN checks, or remote_apply for critical paths.
  • Logical replication (publish/subscribe, CDC) enables major upgrades and selective copies but does not copy DDL.
  • Backups: logical (portable, slow) vs physical (fast, PITR capable). Use pgBackRest/Barman/WAL-G, 3-2-1, and test restores.
  • PITR = base backup + archived WAL to a target time; define RPO and RTO.
  • Failover needs failure detection, a consensus store, promotion, client routing and fencing to avoid split brain.
  • Pool connections (PgBouncer transaction mode) and keep active connections near 2 to 4 per core.
